title: Spam Email Classification
subtitle: From simple rules to reliable decisions
task: Build a filter that catches spam without hiding real messages, then decide where to draw the line.
motivation: We start with a keyword rule anyone could write, see where it fails, and fix one problem at a time: better features, learned word weights, controlled complexity, fair model selection and a decision threshold. The data are 5,574 labelled SMS messages from the UCI SMS Spam Collection. Short texts keep every step easy to inspect; the results do not transfer directly to modern email.

stages.title: Understand the task and the data
stages.description: Write a keyword rule, inspect the dataset, and turn messages into numbers and word vectors.

stages.title: Learn word weights and tune them
stages.description: Fit logistic regression, shrink its weights with regularization, and choose C with cross-validation.

stages.title: Try other classifiers
stages.description: Compare LDA, an additive spline model (GAM) and k-nearest neighbours: same task, different assumptions.

stages.title: Make the final decision
stages.description: Pick a model and threshold on validation data, then evaluate the test set exactly once.

objectives: Explain why accuracy can mislead on imbalanced data, and what train / validation / test are each for.
Turn text into numerical features, word counts and TF–IDF vectors.
Read a logistic prediction as a sum of word contributions, and explain how C changes the weights.
Use cross-validation without leaking information from held-out folds.
Compare logistic regression, LDA, a GAM and KNN by their assumptions and validation results.
Choose a threshold from the precision–recall trade-off and report a one-time test result.
prerequisites: Basic Python and NumPy. From lectures: logistic regression, LDA, GAMs, KNN, regularization, cross-validation and classification metrics.
outcome: An executed notebook with your baselines, model comparisons, chosen threshold, final test result and one limitation of the data.

chapters.title: Start with the inbox
chapters.question: What should a spam filter actually do?
chapters.idea: A spam filter makes decisions, and its two kinds of mistake cost different things.
points: Label spam as 1 and normal messages (ham) as 0.
Two mistakes: blocking a real message (false positive) or letting spam through (false negative). Losing an internship offer is worse than seeing one advert.
The simplest filter: flag a message if it contains a keyword such as free, win or prize. Easy to explain, and easy to fool.
steps: Look at the four example messages. Which decisions are wrong?
Edit the keywords and apply the rule to real validation messages.
Read the mistakes. They motivate the rest of the tutorial.
chapters.takeaway: A rule is a useful baseline. Its mistakes show why we need to combine many pieces of evidence and learn from data.
chapters.experiment: Add or remove one keyword. Which mistakes appear or disappear, and why?
chapters.starter:
keywords = ["free", "win", "prize"]
prediction = rule_predict(X_val, keywords)
print("Rule confusion:", metrics(y_val, prediction)["confusion"])
for text in ["Are you free after class?", "Claim your prize now"]:
    print(text, "→", rule_predict([text], keywords)[0])

chapters.title: Know the data
chapters.question: What does this dataset let us learn?
chapters.idea: Know where the data come from, and keep the test set untouched.
points: UCI SMS Spam Collection (Almeida et al., 2011): 5,574 English text messages, each labelled ham or spam. No email headers or subjects.
Remove 415 duplicate messages before splitting, so the same text can never be in both training and test.
Split 60 / 20 / 20. Train: fit models. Validation: compare models and pick a threshold. Test: use once, at the very end.
Only 12% is spam. Predicting “ham” for everything already scores 87.5% accuracy, and catches no spam at all.
notation: every split keeps the same spam proportion
steps: Look at the raw file, then browse and search the cleaned table.
Follow the counts from the raw file to the three splits.
Compare the always-ham baseline's accuracy with its spam recall.
chapters.takeaway: Accuracy alone can hide a useless filter. Always check the class balance and the spam recall.
chapters.experiment: Compute accuracy and spam recall for the always-ham baseline. Why do we remove duplicates before splitting?
chapters.starter:
print("Training / validation:", len(X_train), len(X_val))
print("Training spam proportion:", y_train.mean())
baseline = metrics(y_val, np.zeros(len(y_val)))
print("Always-ham accuracy:", baseline["accuracy"])
print("Always-ham recall:", baseline["recall"])

chapters.title: Build observable features
chapters.question: What can we measure before understanding language?
chapters.idea: Turn each message into a few numbers a model can use.
points: Measure five things: characters, words, links, digits and exclamation marks.
Spam tends to be longer and to contain more digits (prices, phone numbers), but the two classes overlap.
Counts are skewed, so take log(1+x), then standardize with the training mean and standard deviation.
Five numbers lose most of the meaning: very different messages can share the same counts.
notation: raw count, e.g. number of digits
mean and SD from training data only
steps: Type a message and watch its five numbers.
Compare the ham and spam histograms for each feature.
Fit a logistic model on these five numbers as a baseline.
chapters.takeaway: Every representation keeps some evidence and throws the rest away.
chapters.experiment: Write two very different messages with the same five numbers. What can this representation not see?
chapters.starter:
texts = ["Are you free at 8?", "WIN £1000! Visit https://example.org now!!!"]
print("Characters, words, links, digits, exclamations:")
print(numerical_features(texts))
model = build_model(representation="numeric")
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
print("Numerical baseline AP:", metrics(y_val, model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1])["average_precision"])

chapters.title: Turn words into vectors
chapters.question: How can the model use the actual words?
chapters.idea: Give every word its own column.
points: Split text into lowercase words (tokens). The training vocabulary defines the columns.
Bag of words: each cell counts how often that word appears. Word order is lost.
A new message reuses the same columns. Words not in the vocabulary are ignored.
TF–IDF gives less weight to words that appear in many documents, then scales each row to length 1.
notation: each row is scaled to length 1
steps: Click a word to highlight its column.
Switch between counts and TF–IDF.
Add an unseen word to the new message. Where does it go?
chapters.takeaway: fit learns the vocabulary from training data; transform reuses it. Never refit on new messages.
chapters.experiment: Repeat a word, reorder the sentence, add an unseen word. What changes in counts and in TF–IDF?
chapters.starter:
vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(token_pattern=r"(?u)\b[a-z0-9]+\b")
toy = ["free prize now", "are you free after class", "win a prize prize"]
X = vectorizer.fit_transform(toy)
print("Vocabulary:", vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())
print("IDF:", np.round(vectorizer.idf_, 3))
print("New message:", vectorizer.transform(["free meeting tomorrow"]).toarray())

chapters.title: Learn a weighted rule
chapters.question: How do word counts become a spam score?
chapters.idea: Logistic regression learns how much each word counts as evidence.
points: Score z = bias + Σ weight × feature. Positive terms push towards spam, negative towards ham.
The sigmoid turns z into a probability p. With threshold 0.5: spam exactly when z ≥ 0.
Explain one prediction with its contributions wⱼxⱼ. A word that is not in the message contributes 0.
Training minimizes cross-entropy, as in Tutorial04; sklearn does the optimization.
notation: contribution of word j to this message
steps: Fit a classifier on word counts or TF–IDF.
Read the message's word contributions and where it lands on the sigmoid.
Change one word and predict the new score before you check.
chapters.takeaway: Contributions explain the model's arithmetic, not cause and effect.
chapters.experiment: Swap a spammy word for a normal one. How do the contributions, score and probability change?
chapters.starter:
model = build_model(representation="count", C=1)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
text = "Congratulations claim your free prize now"
x = model[:-1].transform([text])
w = model.named_steps["classifier"].coef_[0]
b = model.named_steps["classifier"].intercept_[0]
z = float((x @ w)[0]) + b
print("Score / probability:", z, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)))
print("Validation AP:", metrics(y_val, model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1])["average_precision"])

chapters.title: Control the fitted rule
chapters.question: Should one rare word receive a huge weight?
chapters.idea: Penalize large weights so that rare words cannot dominate.
points: There are 2,500 word columns but only 385 training spam messages. Some words look decisive just by chance.
The L2 penalty shrinks weights towards 0. In sklearn, smaller C means a stronger penalty.
Too strong: the model underfits. Too weak: it memorizes training noise. Watch the gap between training and validation.
notation: sklearn's inverse penalty: small C, strong penalty
steps: Fit the same model for five values of C.
Follow individual word weights as the penalty weakens.
Compare training and validation AP.
chapters.takeaway: C controls how the model is fitted; the threshold controls decisions afterwards. They are different knobs.
chapters.experiment: Which C gives the best validation AP? Did larger weights help?
chapters.starter:
for C in [.001, .01, .1, 1, 10]:
    model = build_model(C=C)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    p = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
    norm = np.linalg.norm(model.named_steps["classifier"].coef_)
    print(f"C={C:g}, weight norm={norm:.3f}, validation AP={metrics(y_val, p)["average_precision"]:.3f}")

chapters.title: Select with cross-validation
chapters.question: What must be fitted again inside each fold?
chapters.idea: Cross-validation tests the whole pipeline, not just the classifier.
points: Split the training data into 5 folds. Fit on 4, score the 5th, rotate, then average.
The vocabulary and IDF are learned too. Refit them inside every fold, or held-out words leak into training.
Pick the C with the best mean score, then refit on all training data.
notation: average precision on fold f; the pipeline is fitted without it
area-like summary of the precision–recall curve
steps: Pick a held-out fold and see which data fit the pipeline.
Run CV and compare the five fold scores for each C.
Refit the chosen C on all training data.
chapters.takeaway: Leakage-free CV gives a fair choice of C. Only the test set gives the final, unbiased number.
chapters.experiment: Why can the vocabulary size differ between folds, and why is that correct?
chapters.starter:
rows = cross_validate(X_train, y_train, representation="count")
for row in rows:
    print("C / fold AP / mean:", row["C"], np.round(row["folds"], 3), round(row["mean"], 3))
print("Selected C:", max(rows, key=lambda r: r["mean"])["C"])

chapters.title: Model the class distributions
chapters.question: What changes if we model the features within each class?
chapters.idea: LDA models what each class looks like, then applies Bayes' rule.
points: Assume each class is Gaussian, with its own mean and a shared covariance.
A shared covariance makes the boundary linear, like logistic regression, but it is reached differently.
The class prior (88% ham) moves the boundary towards the rarer spam class.
We use the five numerical features; a Gaussian model does not suit 2,500 sparse word counts.
steps: Fit LDA on the five numerical features.
Read the class means, covariance ellipses and boundary.
Compare with numerical logistic regression: same inputs, different model.
chapters.takeaway: Compare models on the same inputs, so that a difference comes from the model and not the features.
chapters.experiment: Compare LDA with logistic regression on the same five features. Which assumption could be wrong here?
chapters.starter:
for kind in ["logistic", "lda"]:
    model = build_model(kind=kind, representation="numeric")
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    p = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
    print(kind, "validation AP:", metrics(y_val, p)["average_precision"])

chapters.title: Allow smooth feature effects
chapters.question: Must each extra character change the score by the same amount?
chapters.idea: Let each feature bend: a smooth curve instead of a straight line.
points: Logistic regression: each feature adds wⱼxⱼ, a straight line in log-odds.
Additive model (GAM): each feature adds its own smooth curve fⱼ, built from spline pieces.
Still additive: no interactions between features.
Here: sklearn SplineTransformer followed by L2-penalized logistic regression.
steps: Fit the additive model on the five numerical features.
Read each curve: where does it bend?
Compare with numerical logistic regression and LDA.
chapters.takeaway: Flexibility can help or overfit. Validation decides.
chapters.experiment: Find a curve that is clearly not straight. What would one constant weight miss?
chapters.starter:
for kind in ["logistic", "gam"]:
    model = build_model(kind=kind, representation="numeric", C=1)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(kind, "validation AP:", metrics(y_val, model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1])["average_precision"])

chapters.title: Learn from similar messages
chapters.question: What makes two messages neighbours?
chapters.idea: KNN classifies a message by asking its k most similar training messages.
points: Nothing to fit: store the training set, find the k nearest, report the spam fraction.
Similarity is a choice: Euclidean distance on standardized numbers, cosine distance on word vectors.
Small k: local and noisy. Large k: smoother, but drifts towards the majority class (ham).
chapters.equation: \hat p(\mathbf x)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in N_k(\mathbf x)}y_i,\qquad d_{\cos}=1-\frac{\mathbf x^\top\mathbf x_i}{\|\mathbf x\|\,\|\mathbf x_i\|}
steps: Choose a representation and k, then fit.
Read the neighbours that voted for your message.
Compare the vote with logistic regression.
chapters.takeaway: Always look at the neighbours: “nearest” does not always mean similar in meaning.
chapters.experiment: Compare k = 3 and k = 15. Which new neighbours join the vote?
chapters.starter:
model = build_model(kind="knn", representation="tfidf", k=5)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
text = "claim your free prize now"
vector = model[:-1].transform([text])
distance, index = model.named_steps["classifier"].kneighbors(vector)
for d, i in zip(distance[0], index[0]):
    print(round(d, 3), "spam" if y_train[i] else "ham", X_train[i])
print("Spam vote:", model.predict_proba([text])[0, 1])

chapters.title: Choose the final decision
chapters.question: How should scores become inbox actions?
chapters.idea: A threshold turns scores into actions. Choose it on validation, then test once.
points: Raise the threshold: fewer messages flagged, so fewer false alarms but more missed spam.
Precision = TP/(TP+FP): of the flagged messages, how many are spam? Recall = TP/(TP+FN): of all spam, how much is caught?
The PR and ROC curves show every threshold at once; average precision (AP) summarizes the ranking.
Write down your choice and reason, then evaluate the test set once.
steps: Pick a candidate model and move the threshold.
Watch the score histograms, confusion matrix and curves change together.
Write your reason, freeze the decision, run the test.
chapters.takeaway: The test result describes this dataset split, not modern email.
chapters.experiment: Justify your threshold with validation evidence. Then report the frozen decision's test result and one limitation of the data.
chapters.starter:
model = build_model(representation="tfidf", C=1)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
p = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
for t in [.2, .5, .8]:
    result = metrics(y_val, p, t)
    print("Threshold:", t, "precision:", round(result["precision"], 3), "recall:", round(result["recall"], 3), "confusion:", result["confusion"])
